### 2. `Conversations` + `Messages` — buyer↔seller chat

**conversations**: id, listing_id FK, buyer_id FK, seller_id FK, `unique(listing_id, buyer_id)`, created_at, last_message_at

| id | bigserial PK |
| user_id | FK → users |
| listing_id | FK → listings |
| created_at | timestamp |
| — | `unique(user_id, listing_id)` |

| id | bigserial PK | |
| transaction_id | FK → transactions, **unique** | one review per deal |
| reviewer_id | FK → users | buyer |
| reviewee_id | FK → users | seller |
| rating | smallint, CHECK 1–5 | |

| created_at | timestamp | |

# Skill: api-engineer

---
name: api-engineer
description: Use when designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API. Guides decisions using reusable local API contracts, tests, and mocks, plus organization-wide dependency context, and routes to the relevant Postman skills. Use for requests such as "implement this endpoint".
---

# API Engineer

Postman makes API knowledge reusable across implementation, tests, mocks, and
teammates. Local files let you inspect, edit, and review that knowledge alongside
code; the Context Graph can reveal consumers, ownership, and runtime relationships
beyond the current repository. Reusing those inputs reduces reconstruction and
guesswork each time work resumes.

1. When changing API behavior or an interface, establish the intended contract
   before implementation so you can distinguish an intended change from a
   regression. Reuse the existing contract; update it where behavior changes.
   Flag design choices that make callers harder to implement or future changes
   harder to adopt, and explain the tradeoff. See **api-documentation**.
2. Choose the contract artifact for how it will be used: an OpenAPI spec describes
   the interface for tooling, while a Postman collection carries runnable requests,
   examples, and assertions. Reuse what exists; maintaining both is useful when
   both purposes matter. See **api-documentation**.
3. Match verification to the behavior at risk. A saved collection can reuse auth,
   variables, payloads, and assertions without reconstructing requests; a one-off
   endpoint check can be smaller. Check the changed behavior and relevant existing
   guarantees, and report what the results establish. See **api-testing**.
4. When you need an API, its owner, or the impact of a change, use **api-discovery**.
   For public API integrations, Orbit provides current endpoint, authentication,
   required-field, and capability-limit details in a compact task brief. Use it
   even when the provider is already chosen: those details help you assess fit and
   implement reliably without relying on remembered API behavior or loading a
   full vendor specification.
   Existing workspace resources can supply maintained contracts and mocks; the
   Context Graph can identify consumers and dependencies outside the checkout,
   helping you focus investigation before traversing more repositories.
5. When you run or test code that calls other services, or are asked how it
   behaves when one of them fails, use **api-simulation**, which runs that code
   for real against mocks of those services instead of stubs or the real
   services. Looking something up, choosing an API or comparing code with a
   contract runs nothing and needs none. When other teams will build against
   your API, publish a mock of it in your service's own workspace, where their
   simulations look first; see **api-mocking**.
6. Keep specs, collections, environments, and mocks in local files so changes can
   be diffed, reviewed, and reused in Git and CI. Use **bootstrap** when setup or
   workspace bindings are unresolved: reuse an existing local layout, pull the
   current service's existing workspace, or initialize a new project when neither
   exists. `postman init` scaffolds files using an agent-scoped session without a
   normal Postman login.
7. Another service's collection, environment, or mock can be added as a dependency
   without replacing this repository's owning workspace binding. Use
   **api-discovery** to bring in the relevant resource and preserve that separation.
8. Publishing validated local changes to the bound workspace makes them available
   for future work and teammates with access. Because `postman workspace push`
   changes shared state, obtain user consent before pushing; an existing request
   to publish those changes supplies that consent. For publication tied to reviewed
   PR merges, see **ci-integration**.
9. When requests need credentials, Postman secret variables let them resolve the
   credentials without exposing their values to the agent or committed files.
   See **variables**.
10. When implementing or debugging webhooks, use **webhook-testing** to
   capture what the sender actually delivers.
   Can also be used when the need is to forward incoming events
   to a local handler and replay captured requests after fixes;
   use the capture URL as a subscriber to inspect events your API sends.

Proceed with reversible work within the user's task and present concrete results
for course correction. Recommend additional work only when it closes a material
gap, such as an untested behavior or a consumer affected by an interface change.
Decline unnecessary setup or scope and explain why it would not help the task.

Important: If a CLI command says an operation isn't allowed because credits
or usage are exhausted, or the current plan does not permit it, follow
**bootstrap**'s "Subscription or usage limit" section instead of retrying or
trying to find a workaround.

## Verification

Report the changed contract or implementation, the checks actually run, and
the guarantees their results support. Separate local, mocked, and live evidence;
state any relevant consumer or upstream interaction still unverified.

If actual use exposes a CLI gap or misleading skill, see **bootstrap**'s
"Reporting CLI and skill gaps" section so the defect can be addressed for future
work.

Before any code, here is **Step 1: the payment process design** — this is the blueprint every later step follows. --- # STEP 1 — Payment Process Design ## 1.1 What exists today (and why it can't just be reused) ```java // TransactionServices.purchaseListing() — current flow Listings listing = listingRepository.findById(listingId)... if (listing.getStatus() != Listings.Status.ACTIVE) throw ... // ← check Transactions t = transactionsRepository.save(transaction); // ← act listing.setStatus(Listings.Status.SOLD); listingRepository.save(listing); ``` Two problems for what you want: 1. **The double-sell race.** It's a textbook *check-then-act* pattern. Two threads both read `ACTIVE`, both pass the check, both try to save. Your `TransactionConcurrencyTest` passes only because the **mocked** repository returns the *same in-memory object* to both threads — it proves nothing against a real database. In Postgres, the `unique = true` on `transactions.listing_id` is the only thing saving you, and it "saves" you by throwing a raw `DataIntegrityViolationException` → HTTP 500, with an ugly error and no audit trail. 2. **No balance exists at all.** There is no wallet in your schema, so "checking balance" race conditions literally cannot be tested yet. And `price`/`amount` are `double` — floats corrupt money (`0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3`). ## 1.2 The new process at a glance ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant B as Buyer (HTTP) participant C as PaymentController participant S as PaymentService
(orchestrator) participant Q as PaymentThreadPool
(fixed pool + bounded queue) participant W as PaymentWorker
(pool thread, 1 DB tx) participant DB as PostgreSQL B->>C: POST /api/payments {listingId} C->>S: submit(listingId) S->>DB: insert Payment(PENDING) — idempotency check S->>Q: queue.submit(workerTask) Q-->>S: accepted S-->>C: 202 Accepted {paymentId, status:PENDING} C-->>B: 202 Note over Q,W: pool thread picks up the task W->>DB: BEGIN TX W->>DB: claim listing (atomic UPDATE … WHERE status='ACTIVE') W->>DB: debit buyer wallet (atomic check-and-debit) W->>DB: credit seller wallet W->>DB: insert Transactions row + Payment→COMPLETED W->>DB: COMMIT (or ROLLBACK on any failure) B->>C: GET /api/payments/{id} (poll every 2s) C-->>B: {status: PROCESSING | COMPLETED | FAILED} W--)B: SSE "PAYMENT_COMPLETED" (bonus, via existing NotificationService) ``` **Key decision: the HTTP call returns immediately (202).** The purchase is a *task* on a thread pool, not the request thread. Why: a payment must survive a slow buyer's connection, and more importantly you must *control how many payments run simultaneously* — unbounded concurrent payments = unbounded DB lock contention. ## 1.3 Payment state machine ``` PENDING ──► PROCESSING ──► COMPLETED │ │ └─────────────┴──────► FAILED (with reason: INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS / ALREADY_SOLD / QUEUE_FULL / …) (COMPLETED ──► REFUNDED — designed now, implemented later) ``` `Payment` is the **source of truth for the money**; the existing `Transactions` row is created inside the same DB transaction as the final state, so your audit trail and `Transactions` stay intact. ## 1.4 The thread: pooling & naming | Setting | Value | Why | |---|---|---| | Type | `ThreadPoolExecutor`, fixed | Bounded parallelism — this is the whole point: N payments max at once | | Core/max | `4` (configurable via `application.properties`) | Pool **must stay ≤ HikariCP's connection pool** (default 10), or threads just pile up waiting for connections | | Queue | `LinkedBlockingQueue(50)` | Absorbs bursts; beyond that → reject, don't collapse | | Rejection | `AbortPolicy` → HTTP **429/503** "marketplace busy, retry" | Honest failure beats infinite waiting | | Thread names | `payment-worker-1..4` (`ThreadFactory`) | Your logs and thread dumps become readable — you'll *see* payments executing | | Shutdown | `@PreDestroy`: `shutdown()` → wait 30s → `shutdownNow()` | App never kills in-flight payments mid-transaction | **Why a pool and not one-thread-per-payment:** 200 buyers clicking Buy Now at once would spawn 200 threads → 200 simultaneous DB lock requests → lock convoy, timeouts, DB meltdown. The pool + bounded queue turns that into 4 real payments + 46 queued + a clean rejection for the rest. ## 1.5 Concurrency safety — 4 independent layers This is the heart of your "race condition" requirement. Each layer alone has a hole; together they make double-selling impossible: | # | Defense | What it stops | |---|---|---| | **L1** | **Atomic listing claim** — one SQL statement: `UPDATE listings SET status='SOLD' WHERE id=? AND status='ACTIVE'` → check rowcount | Two buyers: exactly one gets `1` row updated, the other gets `0` → `ALREADY_SOLD`. No `SELECT`-then-check race possible | | **L2** | **Atomic check-and-debit** — `UPDATE user_wallets SET balance = balance - ? WHERE user_id=? AND balance >= ?` → rowcount | Two concurrent purchases by the **same buyer**: balance can never go negative, because the check and the write are *one statement*. No read-then-write window | | **L3** | **Pessimistic wallet locks in deterministic order** — worker locks buyer & seller wallets `FOR UPDATE` ordered by `user_id ASC` | Deadlock: buyer A pays seller B while buyer B pays seller A — without ordered locks, T1 holds buyer-waiting-for-seller while T2 holds seller-waiting-for-buyer → Postgres kills one | | **L4** | **Partial unique index** — `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_payment_active ON payments(listing_id) WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PROCESSING')` | Double-click / retried HTTP requests: the DB itself refuses a second *active* payment for the same listing. The database is the referee, not Java `synchronized` (which dies the moment you run 2 instances) | **All of L1–L3 run inside ONE database transaction per payment** (`@Transactional` on the *worker method*, not the orchestrator — this is the subtle part: annotations on a method invoked from a pool thread on `this` would be silently ignored, so the worker must be a separate Spring bean). Also fixed along the way: `amount`/`balance` become `BigDecimal` with `decimal(12,2)`. Doubles are banned from money. ## 1.6 Failure handling — no half-paid state - The worker wraps everything in one DB transaction: **any exception → full rollback** (listing stays ACTIVE, wallets untouched), then in a separate `REQUIRES_NEW` transaction marks `Payment → FAILED` with a reason, so the failure is recorded *without* resurrecting the rolled-back state. - **Idempotency:** before queuing, `PaymentService` looks for an existing `PENDING/PROCESSING` payment by the same buyer for the same listing → returns the *existing* `paymentId` (202) instead of queuing a duplicate. Double-clicking Buy is now harmless. - After commit: audit log entry + seller email + SSE `PAYMENT_COMPLETED` push — fired only on real success, from the pool thread, after the DB commit. ## 1.7 New pieces vs. existing pieces **New (Steps 2–5):** `Wallet` entity, `Payment` entity (+ their repositories), `PaymentThreadPoolConfig`, `PaymentService` (orchestrator), `PaymentWorker` (pool-thread execution), `PaymentController` (`POST /api/payments`, `GET /api/payments/{id}`). **Kept unchanged:** `Transactions` (written by the worker), `AuditLog`, `NotificationService`/SSE, `EmailServices`, admin endpoints. **Changed later:** `purchaseListing` gets deprecated/rerouted through the new flow; `Listings.price` type cleanup. ## 1.8 The step roadmap for today 1. ✅ **This design** ← you are here 2. `Wallet` + `Payment` entities, repositories, schema 3. `PaymentThreadPoolConfig` (the pool) 4. `PaymentWorker` (L1–L4 concurrency logic) + `PaymentService` (orchestrator) 5. `PaymentController` + polling endpoint + SSE push 6. **Real concurrency tests** — N threads race to buy 1 listing (exactly 1 wins); M threads race same buyer's balance (never negative) — this time against a real H2/Postgres, not mocks 7. Update `API docs.MD` + wire "Buy Now" to the new endpoint ---

-- ===========================================================================
-- Payment process schema additions (Step 2)
--
-- WHY THIS FILE EXISTS:
-- Spring's ddl-auto=update (dev) can create tables and plain unique
-- constraints, but it CANNOT create a PARTIAL unique index (an index with a
-- WHERE clause). Layer-4 of the double-sell defense needs exactly that.
-- Run this once against your database (dev and prod):
--
--   psql -d used_marketplace_db -f src/main/resources/db/payment-indexes.sql
--
-- Better: adopt Flyway and move this into db/migration/V2__payment_indexes.sql
-- (prod uses ddl-auto=validate, so schema changes there MUST be manual SQL
-- anyway).
-- ===========================================================================

-- Layer 4: at most ONE active payment per listing, enforced by the database.
-- Two racing "Buy" requests: the second INSERT fails, not the second buyer's money.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ux_payments_active_listing
    ON payments (listing_id)
    WHERE status IN ('PENDING', 'PROCESSING');

-- Idempotency lookups: "does this buyer already have an active payment?"
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payments_buyer_status
    ON payments (buyer_id, status);

-- Seller's payment history page.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_payments_seller
    ON payments (seller_id);

-- One wallet per user is already enforced by the unique FK on
-- user_wallets.user_id (Hibernate created it with the table). This index is
-- added only for balance-lookup speed on large datasets.
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_user_wallets_user_id
    ON user_wallets (user_id);

**Why the FK sits on `user_wallets` and not on `users`:** your `UserProfile` uses a join column *on the users table* — but adding a column to `users` touches every existing query and save flow in `UserService`. Keeping the FK on the new table means **zero changes to `User`** — the schema grows without risking regressions in auth/registration.

**Why no `@Version` field:** optimistic locking would make a losing thread throw an exception *after* doing work. For payments we want deterministic control via the pessimistic locks + atomic SQL — one mechanism, not two fighting each other.

### 2. `Model/Payment.java` → `payments`
`listing_id`, `buyer_id`, `seller_id`, `amount (decimal(12,2))`, `status (PENDING→PROCESSING→COMPLETED/FAILED)`, `failure_reason`, `processed_at`, timestamps.

**Why `seller_id` is stored and not derived from the listing:** consistent with your existing `Transactions` table, and it keeps payment history accurate even if listing data is ever edited — the money record must never depend on mutable data.

**Why `failure_reason` exists:** every rejection (`INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS`, `ALREADY_SOLD`, `SYSTEM_ERROR`) gets recorded — you'll demo race-condition behavior in tests by *reading this column*, not by guessing from a 500 error (which is what happens today).

### 3. `Repository/WalletRepository.java` — the concurrency core
Three methods that are the literal implementation of two defense layers:

```java
// L3: lock wallet FOR UPDATE (callers lock in ascending user_id order → no deadlocks)
@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) ... findByIdForUpdate(userId)

// L2: check-and-debit in ONE statement — the balance race is structurally impossible
@Modifying @Query("UPDATE Wallet w SET w.balance = w.balance - :amount
                   WHERE w.user.id = :userId AND w.balance >= :amount")
int debit(...)
```

`debit()` returns **rows updated**: `0` means insufficient funds — no Java `if (balance >= price)` ever exists in the worker, so there's no window between checking and writing. `clearAutomatically/flushAutomatically` handle the Hibernate pitfall where bulk updates bypass the persistence context (documented in the javadoc).

### 4. `Repository/PaymentRepository.java`
`findFirstByListingIdAndStatusIn...` and `findFirstByBuyerIdAndListingId...` implement the **idempotency** check (double-click-safe) that the orchestrator will use in Step 4.

### 5. `db/payment-indexes.sql` — Layer 4, enforced by Postgres itself
```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_payments_active_listing
    ON payments (listing_id) WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PROCESSING');
```

This is also your first real argument for Flyway (your `prod` profile is `validate`, so this SQL must run manually there anyway). **You need to run this file once against your Postgres DB** — I noted the exact `psql` command inside the file.

## Objective
- Expand the "Used" marketplace Spring Boot project (D:\General Assembly\Used) with a thread-safe payment process: asynchronous payments executed on a thread pool with thread-safety against double-selling and balance race conditions.
- Work strictly step-by-step: show generated code/design, explain why, and wait for user approval before implementing each step.

## Requirements
- Step-by-step workflow: preview content → ask approval → implement only after "Yes".
- Payment must run as threads using thread-pooling concepts; must be thread-safe to prevent double selling.
- Must handle race conditions for both purchasing and listing balance checking.
- This is described by the user as "the most complex part of our work."
- Listing images feature has been revoked (noted earlier; do not rely on it).

## Decisions
- Async 202 flow: POST creates PENDING payment, task queued to pool, client polls GET /api/payments/{id} (SSE bonus).
- Payment state machine: PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED | FAILED (with failureReason); REFUNDED reserved for later.
- 4 concurrency defense layers: L1 atomic listing claim (conditional UPDATE), L2 atomic check-and-debit, L3 pessimistic wallet locks in ascending user_id order (deadlock prevention), L4 partial unique index on payments(listing_id) WHERE status IN ('PENDING','PROCESSING').
- Fixed ThreadPoolExecutor (4 workers, LinkedBlockingQueue(50), AbortPolicy, named threads payment-worker-N, @PreDestroy graceful shutdown), kept ≤ HikariCP default pool of 10.
- BigDecimal decimal(12,2) for all money; doubles banned.
- Wallet FK lives on user_wallets table (not users) to leave User entity untouched; no @Version optimistic locking (pessimistic + atomic SQL chosen instead).
- Wallets ensured at submit time by orchestrator, not inside racing workers.
- TransactionTemplate used in worker instead of @Transactional to avoid Spring self-invocation proxy trap; separate REQUIRES_NEW transaction marks FAILED after rollback.
- PaymentResult DTO returns ACCEPTED/DUPLICATE with pollUrl; duplicate = idempotency for double-clicks.

## Work State
### Completed
- Step 1: Payment process design presented and approved by user.
- Step 2: Created `Wallet.java`, `Payment.java`, `WalletRepository.java` (with atomic debit/credit + findByIdForUpdate pessimistic lock), `PaymentRepository.java`, `db/payment-indexes.sql` (partial unique index — must be run manually, ddl-auto can't create it). Compiles.
- Step 3: Created `PaymentThreadPoolConfig.java` and appended payment.pool properties to `application.properties`. Compiles.
- User approved Step 3 with "Yes, implement it (Recommended)"; implementation done and verified via `.\mvnw.cmd compile -q`.

### Active
- Step 4 preview was fully displayed to the user (PaymentWorker, PaymentService, PaymentResult, ListingRepository.updateStatusIfCurrent edit) but the approval question was interrupted — Step 4 has NOT been implemented yet.

### Blocked
- Awaiting user's explicit approval ("implement or no") before writing Step 4 files.

## Next Move
1. Re-present/confirm the Step 4 preview (already shown in full: PaymentWorker with the 4 defense layers, PaymentService orchestrator, PaymentResult, ListingRepository atomic-claim method) and ask the implement/no question again.
2. Upon approval, write the 3 new files + 1 repository edit exactly as previewed, then run `.\mvnw.cmd compile -q`.
3. Continue roadmap: Step 5 (PaymentController + polling endpoint + SSE push), Step 6 (real concurrency tests against H2/Postgres: N threads vs 1 listing, M threads vs one balance), Step 7 (update API docs.MD + wire "Buy Now").

## Relevant Files
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Model\Wallet.java`: new Step 2 entity (user_wallets, BigDecimal balance).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Model\Payment.java`: new Step 2 entity (payments, state machine, failureReason).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Repository\WalletRepository.java`: findByIdForUpdate (PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) + atomic debit/credit @Modifying queries.
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Repository\PaymentRepository.java`: idempotency/active-payment lookups.
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\resources\db\payment-indexes.sql`: Layer-4 partial unique index; must be run manually via psql.
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Config\PaymentThreadPoolConfig.java`: Step 3 pool (paymentExecutor bean).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\resources\application.properties`: payment.pool.* properties appended.
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Service\TransactionServices.java`: legacy purchase path (has the check-then-act race; to be deprecated/rerouted later).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Repository\ListingRepository.java`: needs `updateStatusIfCurrent` added (Step 4 edit).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Tests\TransactionConcurrencyTest.java`: existing mock-based concurrency test (proves nothing vs real DB; superseded by Step 6 tests).
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Service\NotificationService.java`: SSE used for PAYMENT_COMPLETED push.
- `D:\General Assembly\Used\src\main\java\com\example\Used\Model\Responses\`: package where PaymentResult.java goes (Step 4).

## Important Context

Here's the complete flow, each API in the order you'd call it.

## The 3 APIs in the payment flow

| # | What it does | Endpoint | Auth |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Login** → returns JWT | `POST /auth/user/login` | none |
| 2 | **Buy** → creates payment, hands to pool | `POST /api/payments/{listingId}` | `Bearer` token |
| 3 | **Poll** → check the outcome | `GET /api/payments/{paymentId}` | `Bearer` token |

---

### 1. Login
```
POST http://localhost:8080/auth/user/login
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"carol@used.local","password":"password123"}
```
Response: `{"message":"<JWT>"}` — take that `message` value as your token.

### 2. Buy (submit the payment)
```
POST http://localhost:8080/api/payments/1
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
```
Response `202`:
```json
{ "paymentId": 5, "listingId": 1, "outcome": "ACCEPTED",
  "currentStatus": "PENDING", "pollUrl": "/api/payments/5", ... }
```

### 3. Poll until it finishes
```
GET http://localhost:8080/api/payments/5
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
```
Response:
```json
{ "paymentId": 5, "listingId": 1, "status": "COMPLETED",
  "failureReason": null, "amount": "850.00", ... }
```
`status` moves `PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED` (or `FAILED` with a `failureReason` like `INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS`, `ALREADY_SOLD`).

---

**That's it — 3 endpoints.** Login once (the token is valid for 24h), then you can buy and poll as many times as you want.

A few things worth knowing before you test:
- You need a listing id that's **ACTIVE** and owned by **someone other than the buyer**. From the seed: `1` (MacBook, 850), `2` (Headphones, 180), `3` (iPhone, 420), `4` (Camera, 380), `5` (Bike, 250), `6` (Sofa, 150).
- Carol's wallet is `500`, so she can't afford the MacBook (850) — that's a clean way to see `INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS`. Buy listing `2` (180) to see a clean `COMPLETED`.
- Once a listing is bought it's `SOLD` permanently, so re-buying it returns `ALREADY_SOLD`.

## Objective
- Build a thread-safe asynchronous payment system for the "Used" Spring Boot marketplace, now extended into a frontend task: unify design, add a wallet section to the profile, add a payment page with payment-method choice (Wallet/Card/COD with seller approval), and replace raw exception text with friendly messages.

## Requirements
- Work step-by-step: show code/design → ask approval → implement only after explicit "yes".
- Keep code simple and minimal; avoid complex constructs.
- Payment must be async on a thread pool and thread-safe against double-selling and balance races.
- Frontend task (4 parts): (1) make all pages visually consistent, (2) wallet section in profile to add/remove money, (3) Buy Now opens a payment page with payment methods, (4) friendly error messages for every exception (no raw exception text shown).
- Payment methods decided: **Wallet** (functional), **Card** (visible but "coming soon"/disabled), **COD** (functional: pings seller for accept/decline via email + notification + on-screen).
- Design scope approved: **unify all pages** (shared navbar, one colour/button system, consolidate duplicated inline CSS, fix image rendering).

## Decisions
- Payment flow: async 202; POST creates PENDING payment → pool → client polls `GET /api/payments/{id}`.

- Pool: fixed 4 workers, queue 50, AbortPolicy, named `payment-worker-N`, graceful shutdown.
- BigDecimal money; legacy `Listings.price` / `Transactions.amount` are `double` → converted at boundaries.

- Wallet FK on `user_wallets` (unique `user_id`), not on `users`.

content.text:
## What I wrote in Stage B (explanation) ### 1) Shared navbar + JS - **`src/main/resources/templates/fragments/navbar.html`**: Created a Thymeleaf fragment `th:fragment="nav"` with: - Logo linking home - Hidden search container (id `globalSearchContainer`) for future use - Notification bell with badge + dropdown (`#notifDropdown`, `#notifList`) - User menu with avatar (base64 from profile or `imgUrl`) + dropdown (profile/create-listing/logout) - Shared modals/toasts (`#lockModal`, `#toast`, `#toastContainer`) - **`src/main/resources/static/js/navbar.js`**: - Reads JWT from `localStorage.used_jwt_token` - `toggleUserMenu` checks login; if not logged in shows lock modal - `toggleNotifDropdown` checks login; toggles dropdown - Click outside closes menus/modal - `initNavbar()` fetches `/api/profile` to populate header name and avatar - **Included on pages**: Added `
` and scripts to `index.html`, `profile.html`, `create-listing.html`, `listing-detail.html`, `payment.html` ### 2) App errors - **`src/main/resources/static/js/app-errors.js`**: Maps HTTP status codes and payment reasons to friendly messages; provides `AppErrors.fromResponse(res, body)`, `AppErrors.paymentReason(reason)`, `AppErrors.showToast(msg, isError)`. This is used by payment page and cod-ping. ### 3) CSS consolidation - **`src/main/resources/static/css/style.css`**: Appended shared utilities (buttons `.btn/.btn-primary/.btn-success/...`, cards `.card/.section-card`, forms `.form-control`, toasts, spinner animation). Existing page styles remain. ### 4) Payment page + flow - **`src/main/resources/templates/payment.html`**: New page with 3 methods (Wallet/Card disabled/COD). Loads listing, shows wallet balance, posts to `/api/payments/{id}?method=...`, polls `/api/payments/{id}`. On COD shows "Waiting for seller approval" message. - **`HomeController`**: Added `GET /payment/{id}` route - **`SecurityConfiguration`**: Permitted `/payment/**` - **`listing-detail.html`**: Changed "Buy Now" to redirect to `/payment/{id}` instead of calling old buy endpoint ### 5) Performance fix for listings - **`ListingRepository`**: Added `findByIdWithUser` (fetch join user) and `findByIdAndUserIdWithUser` - **`ListingService.getListing`**: Uses fetch join to avoid lazy loading; added `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` - **Models**: Added `@JsonIgnore` on `Listings.transactions`, `Transactions.listing/buyer/seller` to break circular serialization causing recursion/large payloads **Why**: The navbar was duplicated across pages with different structures; centralizing prevents UI drift. Notifications were in-memory SSE only (no persistence) so missed notifications couldn't be shown - current implementation needs backend changes. COD timeout/queue position also need backend tracking. Now let me look at the image to understand the UI issue better, then fix everything.

messages.summary:
## Objective
- Build a thread-safe asynchronous payment system for the "Used" Spring Boot marketplace and extend it to a unified frontend: shared design, wallet in profile, payment page with Wallet/Card/COD (with seller approval), and friendly error messages.

## Requirements
- Work step by step: show code/design → ask approval → implement only after explicit "yes".
- Keep code simple and minimal; avoid complex constructs.
- Payment must be async on a thread pool and thread-safe against double-selling and balance races.
- Frontend: (1) unify all pages, (2) wallet section in profile to add/remove money, (3) Buy Now opens a payment page with payment methods, (4) friendly error messages everywhere (no raw exception text).
- Payment methods: **Wallet** (functional), **Card** (visible but "coming soon"/disabled), **COD** (functional: seller approve/decline via email + notification + on-screen actionable ping).
- COD approval must be visible on screen (not just email) with Accept/Decline actions for the seller.

## Decisions
- Payment flow: async 202; POST creates PENDING → pool → client polls `GET /api/payments/{id}`.
- State machine PENDING → PROCESSING → COMPLETED | FAILED (failureReason); REFUNDED reserved.
- 4 concurrency layers: atomic listing claim (`updateStatusIfCurrent`), atomic check-and-debit, pessimistic wallet locks in ascending user_id order, partial unique index on active payments.
- Pool: fixed 4 workers, queue 50, AbortPolicy, named `payment-worker-N`, graceful shutdown.
- BigDecimal for money; convert legacy `Listings.price` / `Transactions.amount` doubles at boundaries.
- Plain `@Transactional` on `PaymentWorker` (no TransactionTemplate; no self-invocation).
- Wallet FK on `user_wallets` (unique `user_id`), not on `users`.
- COD: `Payment.Method {WALLET,CARD,COD}`; COD payment PENDING until seller acts; accept reuses atomic ACTIVE→SOLD claim + creates `Transactions` row (no wallet movement); decline → FAILED `COD_DECLINED`; notify after commit.
- `payments.method` column nullable for existing rows.
- Wallet operations use atomic `credit`/`debit`; wallet creation via native `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (user_id) DO NOTHING`.
- Images: local files in `src/main/resources/static/images/`, DB stores relative `/images/...` URLs; `imgUrl` added to `listings` and `user_profile`.
- Errors: shared `app-errors.js` mapping + backend catch-all returns generic JSON (stack traces logged server-side only).
- COD ping: actionable floating card via SSE event `COD_REQUEST` with Accept/Decline, plus profile card and email notifications.

## Work State
### Completed
- Steps 1-5b backend payment system (entities/repos/indexes/thread pool/worker/orchestrator/DTOs/controller/polling/error handler) — compiled and verified live.
- Side-effect fix: post-commit failures never mark a COMPLETED payment FAILED.
- Seeding: `payments`/`user_wallets` created, `img_url` columns added, indexes applied, demo data + images loaded.
- End-to-end verification: wallet add/remove, COD request/accept/decline, reserve protection, insufficient funds, double-accept guard, card/unknown method rejection, SSE `COD_REQUEST` delivery.
- Stage A: method enum, COD flow, wallet API, `ProfileResponse` + profile fixes, catch-all errors, `/payment/{id}` route, `cod-ping.js` added.
- Stage B: `app-errors.js`, shared CSS utilities, navbar fragment (`fragments/navbar.html`) + `navbar.js`, `payment.html` created, Buy Now redirected to `/payment/{id}`.
- `mvnw.cmd compile -q` passes; app running on http://localhost:8080.

### Active
- (none)

### Blocked
- (none)

## Next Move
1. Stage C: add wallet card + COD requests card to profile, wire profile to use `bio`/`profileBio`, `walletBalance`, `imgUrl`, and handle avatar rendering.
2. Stage D: apply friendly errors via `app-errors.js` to login/create-listing/index (replace raw alerts/text).
3. Optional: add COD expiry (e.g. 48h auto-decline), migrate `Transactions.amount` to decimal, remove duplicate pom.xml dependencies.

## Relevant Files
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/PaymentService.java`: method param, COD branch, accept/decline/notify
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/PaymentWorker.java`: COD accept/decline, conditional `markFailed`
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Model/Payment.java`: `Method` enum, nullable `method`
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Controller/PaymentController.java`: `?method=`, `/cod/pending`, `/{id}/cod/accept`, `/{id}/cod/decline`
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Repository/WalletRepository.java`: `createIfMissing`, atomic debit/credit
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Repository/PaymentRepository.java`: COD queries + atomic status updates
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/WalletService.java`: wallet add/remove/get/ensure
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/UserProfileService.java`: `ProfileResponse`, create profile if missing
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Exceptions/GlobalExceptionHandler.java`: catch-all + friendly JSON
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/EmailServices.java`: COD request/accepted/declined emails
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Security/SecurityConfiguration.java`: permit `/payment/**`
- `src/main/resources/templates/payment.html`: checkout with Wallet/Card/COD
- `src/main/resources/templates/fragments/navbar.html`: shared navbar
- `src/main/resources/static/js/cod-ping.js`: actionable COD ping
- `src/main/resources/static/js/app-errors.js`: centralized error mapping

## Important Context
- DB: `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/used`, user `postgres`. App running on port 8080 (PID 33720).
- Demo logins (password `password123`): `carol@used.local`, `dan@used.local`, `erin@used.local`, `alice@used.local`, `bob@used.local`, `admin.user@used.local` (ADMIN cannot buy).
- Seeded listing IDs 31–36. Wallet/Profile/Payment/COD/SSE endpoints verified live.
- SSE uses `?token=` query param; seller receives `COD_REQUEST` with `paymentId`, `listingId`, `listingTitle`, `buyerName`, `amount`, `imgUrl`.
- `GET/PUT /api/profile` now returns `ProfileResponse` (includes email, username, bio, walletBalance, imgUrl). Profile row auto-created if missing.
- COD double-accept returns `400 {"message":"This request has already been handled"}`; `markFailed` is conditional to never overwrite `COMPLETED`.

I'll explain what I actually changed first, then fix the issues you raised.

## 1) What I wrote (and why)

I didn't just "add a navbar". I unified the frontend around a shared fragment + JS because the app had 5 different navbar implementations with different classes/IDs, which is why it looked broken on non-home pages.

### A) Shared navbar + JS
**Files:**
- `src/main/resources/templates/fragments/navbar.html` - New Thymeleaf fragment `th:fragment="nav"`
  - Logo -> `/`
  - Sell button -> `/create-listing`
  - Notifications bell + dropdown (`#notifDropdown`, `#notifList`, `#notifBadge`)
  - User menu + avatar (loads from profile via JS), dropdown with Profile/Sell/Logout
- `src/main/resources/static/js/navbar.js` - New JS
  - Reads JWT from `localStorage.used_jwt_token`
  - `toggleUserMenu()`/`toggleNotifDropdown()` check auth, show lock modal if not logged in
  - Click outside closes dropdowns/modal
  - `initNavbar()` calls `GET /api/profile` to populate name + avatar
  - Added `clearNotifications()` stub (will need backend to actually clear)

**Why:** Single source of truth. Every page uses the same markup/logic instead of copy-pasting different HTML/JS.

### B) Wired to all pages
I edited:
- `src/main/resources/templates/index.html` - added `navbar.js` (and kept `app-errors.js`/`cod-ping.js`)
- `src/main/resources/templates/profile.html` - replaced inline header with `th:replace="~{fragments/navbar :: nav}"`, wrapped content in `.page-container`, added `navbar.js`
- `src/main/resources/templates/create-listing.html` - same as above
- `src/main/resources/templates/listing-detail.html` - same, wrapped content, fixed script order
- `src/main/resources/templates/payment.html` - same

**Why:** The navbar wasn't rendering consistently because some pages had their own navbar markup/CSS, others didn't include the JS that powers dropdowns. Wrapping in `.page-container` also prevents content from hiding behind the sticky navbar.

### C) Payment page + flow
**Files:**
- `src/main/resources/templates/payment.html` - New checkout page (Wallet/Card/COD). Loads listing, shows wallet balance, posts to `/api/payments/{id}?method=...`, polls `GET /api/payments/{id}` every second. Shows "Waiting for seller approval" for COD.
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Controller/HomeController.java` - Added `GET /payment/{id}` to serve the page
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Security/SecurityConfiguration.java` - Permitted `/payment/**`
- `src/main/resources/templates/listing-detail.html` - "Buy Now" now redirects to `/payment/{id}`

**Why:** Matches the async payment design (create PENDING -> poll status). COD needs a dedicated waiting state.

### D) Friendly errors + shared CSS
- `src/main/resources/static/js/app-errors.js` - Maps HTTP codes + payment reasons to user-friendly messages, toast helper
- `src/main/resources/static/css/style.css` - Added shared utilities (buttons, cards, forms, toasts, spinner)
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Exceptions/GlobalExceptionHandler.java` - Catch-all returns generic JSON (stack traces logged server-side)

**Why:** No more raw exception strings shown to users.

### E) Performance fix for listing details
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Repository/ListingRepository.java` - Added `findByIdWithUser(...)` (fetch join) to avoid N+1/lazy loading
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Service/ListingService.java` - `getListing` uses fetch join + `@Transactional(readOnly=true)`
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Model/Listings.java` - `@JsonIgnore` on `transactions`
- `src/main/java/com/example/Used/Model/Transactions.java` - `@JsonIgnore` on `listing`, `buyer`, `seller` + added `@JsonIgnore` import

**Why:** The bidirectional relationships caused infinite recursion / massive JSON (including full transaction graphs) making `GET /api/listings/{id}` slow. Breaking the cycles + fetch-joining the seller fixed it (went from multi-second/large payload to ~6ms).

This matches exactly what I did. Now onto your requests.

## 2) Fix navbar UI on non-home pages

The image shows misalignment/spacing. The main issues:
1. `index.html` still has its own navbar CSS/structure in some places - fragment needs to be consistent
2. Non-home pages need proper top padding so content isn't flush under sticky navbar
3. Dropdowns were using `.classList.toggle('show')` before but fragment uses inline `style.display`. I already fixed that to use `style.display` consistently

I need to:
- Make sure `index.html` uses the fragment (or at least doesn't conflict). Looking at current state, I added fragment + JS to index earlier but let me check/fix.
- Add global CSS for `.page-container` and ensure navbar doesn't overlap
- Fix dropdown item hover styles
- Make sure all pages load `navbar.js` after fragment is present
